title: ASP.NET Product Catalog & Ordering Website
description: Around 2005 I redesigned and rebuilt the main public Essential Skills website in C# and ASP.NET. The site presented the company's software catalog, loaded product information and pricing dynamically from SQL Server, and supported school purchasing through quote requests and purchase-order forms rather than credit-card checkout. I also built the internal product-management backend used to add, update, and remove products and pricing.

sections.title: Main Public Company Website
paragraphs: This was the primary consumer-facing Essential Skills website for that generation.
It acted as the company's public software catalog and purchasing entry point rather than only as a static marketing site.

sections.title: ASP.NET / C# Web Generation
paragraphs: I rebuilt the site during the period when ASP.NET was becoming a major Microsoft web-development platform.
The application was written in C# and ASP.NET and hosted on the company's own Windows Server / IIS infrastructure.

sections.title: Reusable Site Shell
paragraphs: The site used a common page structure where the header, footer, and navigation remained consistent while the page title and content area changed.
This avoided rebuilding common navigation and layout elements across individual product pages.

sections.title: Dynamic Product Catalog
paragraphs: Product names, descriptions, pricing, and related catalog information were loaded dynamically from SQL Server rather than being hard-coded into individual pages.

sections.title: Quote & Purchase Order Workflow
paragraphs: The site supported school purchasing, but not through instant credit-card checkout.
Customers submitted quote requests or purchase-order information, which matched the way schools typically bought higher-priced educational software at the time.

sections.title: High-Value School Purchases
paragraphs: Individual programs could cost thousands of dollars, so purchasing was handled as a considered institutional transaction rather than impulse e-commerce.
Orders were processed offline after submission.

sections.title: Order Submission
paragraphs: Customer order information was submitted through the website and was definitely emailed internally for follow-up.
Jamie also remembers the site likely storing order data in SQL Server, but that specific storage detail is less certain than the email workflow.

sections.title: Product Administration Backend
paragraphs: I built an internal administration interface for maintaining the public catalog.
items: Maintain product descriptions and catalog data

sections.title: SQL Server
paragraphs: SQL Server stored the product/catalog data used by the public website and administration tools.
The system represented one of my early substantial web/database applications using the Microsoft stack.

sections.title: Solo Development
paragraphs: I implemented the site myself even though I was already working with other developers at the company.
The public site, catalog integration, ordering workflow, database integration, and product-administration backend were all part of my work.

sections.title: UI/UX Design
paragraphs: I designed the overall visual presentation and user experience.
The side-menu swirl motif was based on an idea from an earlier company website. I redrew and reinterpreted it, but the original visual concept was not mine.

sections.title: In-House Hosting
paragraphs: The site ran on Essential Skills' own in-house Windows Server and IIS infrastructure rather than on later cloud-hosted infrastructure.

sections.title: Possible ASP.NET Web Forms
paragraphs: ASP.NET Web Forms sounds consistent with Jamie's memory of the implementation, but the exact ASP.NET application model is not remembered strongly enough to state as a confirmed fact without source-code evidence.

sections.title: Frequent Website Redesigns
paragraphs: Essential Skills treated the public website somewhat like a continuously changing company brochure and redesigned it frequently, often roughly yearly.
Jamie was responsible for several website generations over the years, but not every redesign.

sections.title: Short-Lived Website Generation
paragraphs: This ASP.NET generation probably remained the main public site for only several months to around a year before another redesign replaced it.
The exact end date is not remembered.

sections.title: Eventually Outsourced
paragraphs: The company eventually outsourced much of the public-website work because the constant redesign cycle was consuming too much internal development time.

sections.title: Career Significance
paragraphs: This project is useful as a distinct portfolio entry because it captures a substantial early web/database phase in C# and ASP.NET before Jamie's later PHP, JavaScript, AngularJS, React, and broader full-stack work.
